1. Introduction

The decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Saroj Pandey v. Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi [2026] 185 taxmann.com 280 (SC) is a significant pronouncement on the nuanced issue of liability of directors under fiscal and penal laws. At a time when regulatory enforcement is becoming increasingly stringent, the judgment provides much-needed clarity on the extent to which individuals occupying managerial positions can be fastened with liability for acts of a company.

The judgment lays down the boundaries to the extent to which directors are liable and more specifically when they are not liable for the act of the Company being a separate legal entity. Though rendered in the context of Section 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (“N.I. Act”), commonly associated with cheque dishonour cases, the underlying reasoning transcends the statute. The principles articulated by the Court are of wider relevance and have direct bearing on fiscal statutes, including the CGST Act, where similar provisions impose vicarious liability.

2. Concept of Separate Legal Entity and Role of Directors

The doctrine of separate legal entity, firmly embedded in company law jurisprudence since the landmark decision of the House of Lords in Salomon v. Salomon (1897) A.C. 22) followed by the Indian Supreme Court in a plethora of judgements including in the famous Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India [2012] 17 taxmann.com 202 (SC)/[2012] 204 Taxman 408 (SC)/[2012] 341 ITR 1 (SC), recognises a company as a juristic person distinct from its shareholders and directors. This principle has significant implications in fiscal jurisprudence as well, where the company is treated as an independent taxable entity, capable of owning property, incurring liabilities, and being assessed in its own name. Consequently, tax obligations—whether under direct or indirect tax regimes—are ordinarily fastened upon the company itself, and not upon those who manage its affairs. The sanctity of this principle ensures commercial certainty and facilitates risk-taking by insulating individuals from personal exposure arising out of corporate operations.

However, the role of directors introduces a nuanced dimension to this doctrine. While directors act as the “directing mind and will” of the company, their liability in tax matters is not automatic but arises only in specific statutory or exceptional circumstances. Tax statutes, including provisions under the Income-tax Act and GST laws, carve out limited situations where directors may be held personally liable—typically where there is evidence of fraud, wilful default, misfeasance, or where statutory dues cannot be recovered from the company. Even in such cases, the law requires strict compliance with conditions precedent before piercing the corporate veil, thereby maintaining a careful balance between accountability and the foundational principle of separate legal personality.

Judicial trends have consistently underscored that lifting the corporate veil is an exception rather than the rule, to be invoked sparingly and only where the corporate form is abused to evade tax or perpetrate illegality. Courts have cautioned against a routine attribution of liability to directors merely on account of their position, emphasising that vicarious liability must be expressly provided by statute and cannot be inferred. Thus, while directors play a central role in corporate governance and decision-making, their personal exposure in tax matters remains circumscribed, reinforcing that the company—being a separate legal entity—continues to bear primary responsibility for its fiscal obligations.

3. Factual Background

Coming to the case in hand, the appellant was one of the directors of the accused company which had issued cheques towards payment for supply of goods. The cheques were dishonoured upon presentation, following which statutory notice was issued and criminal proceedings were initiated. The director was arrayed as an accused primarily on the ground that she had signed a Board Resolution, which, according to the complainant, demonstrated her involvement in the affairs of the company. This reasoning found favour both with the Magistrate and the High Court, leading to the continuation of proceedings against her.

4. Provision Relating to Prosecution of Director

Section 141 of the N.I. Act, provides the statutory framework for fastening vicarious liability upon directors and officers of a company. The provision makes it clear that liability is not automatic but conditional upon the person being “in charge of” and “responsible to” the company for the conduct of its business at the relevant time. The provisos further carve out safeguards, including absence of knowledge and exercise of due diligence.

A striking feature of the present discussion is the similarity between Section 141 of the N.I. Act and Section 137 of the CGST Act. Both provisions employ nearly identical language in attributing liability to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business, while also recognising defences based on lack of knowledge and due diligence.

Penalty v. Prosecution – Section 142

4. Out of the above provisions, the important provision in section 142 dealing with Penalty and prosecution for defaults in compliance of the provisions of section 138. The important ingredient to complete an offence under section 138 of the Act is the failure of the accused to make payment within 15 days after service of notice. Does Criminal Liability has Solved the Problem?

6. The criminal liability under section 138 has not solved the problem of cheque bouncing and did not develop faith in this credit instrument among the people who widely use it. Our judiciary has played a crucial role by imposing strict liability when the cheque is dishonoured but it does not work effectively and still the cheques are getting dishonoured. It is evident from the fact that Courts are overburdened due to the complaints of dishonour of cheques in spite of law in this regard.

(a) The Act - A failure - It is sadly submitted that the Act is a failure; numerous factors have contributed to this failure. The structural flaws intrinsic in the Act caused its failure, more than anything else, but the larger reason of failure is socio-culture.

The activity which the Act was enacted to remove is still rampant. In other words, people still choose to gather cash in the discharge of obligations owed to them in preference to cheque. It is general place to get that people still hold large amount of cash in settlement of financial obligations and in consummation of commercial activities. The foremost reason for the preference for cash is a lack of confidence in the use of cheques. This lack of confidence is primarily due to the continuing prevalence of dishonoured cheques.

(i) Socio Cultural Impediment - The failure of the Act has more sociological and cultural bases than structural defects inbuilt in the Act. Indians do have extremely small regard for the imperatives of discharging their financial obligations. They think nothing erroneous in issuing a cheque for the reason of discharging their financial obligations that they know will be dishonoured on presentation for insufficiency of funds in their bank accounts. This is a constituent of the encompassing widespread corruption that damages the foundation of Indian society. They don’t file a complaint for being issued a dishonoured cheque in the court, but would rather find other means of getting back debts owed to them by the drawers of the cheque.

There is a dearth of reported cases of the offence created in the Act and by implication, of prosecution of cases under the Act. There is an urgent need to amend the Act.

(ii) Adequacy of the Penalty - The punishment provided by the Act has become dreadfully low and reflects very little significance about limiting the criminal behaviour to which the Act is committed. Only two years imprisonment has been provided which seems to be very less in view of the wrong.

(iii) Cognizance of offences - The procedure provided under section 142 of the Act is not friendly and viable because it provides that the Court will take cognizance of offence or complaint only in writing. Its merely cumbersome formality. The Court should take the cognizance of offences or complaint in oral also as provided under section 200 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973.

India, from the past 3 decades have been imprisoning defaulter, in cases of dishonoring of Cheque, nevertheless having an international obligation of not doing so. Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, of which India too is a party, explicitly outlaws the construct of imprisoning the person for not fulfilling or failing to discharge their contractual obligation; the rationale behind it is that imprisoning such parties will serve no social purpose even after attaching all their property or assets have been attached and possessed by their creditor. Recently, the Center has proposed to decriminalize the dishonoring of cheque coupled with other minor offences. The rationale given for such proposal was that criminal liabilities for minor offences act as deterrents, and this is perceived as one the major reasons impacting business sentiment and hindering investments both from domestic and foreign investors; eventually, this will facilitate unclogging the court process as according to a 213th Law Commission Report, there is about 40 lakh pending dishonor of cheque cases. Recently, the Confederation of All India Trader (CAIT) penned down a letter to the Finance Minister urging to address the issue of rising menace of dishonored cheque hampering the credibility of the crucial payment instrument in the trade ecosystem. The letter in addition to this also cited an observation made by erstwhile Justice Adarsh Kumar Goel, observing that the impugned offence must be decriminalized to lift the burden from the judiciary system1. Whether the cheque dishonor should be decriminalized or not, has become a contemporary issue across India. As to the other developed nations, a cheque is a civil offence. Many civilized nations have already done away with the idea of putting their citizens behind the bars because of their inability to discharge their contractual debts. In India, Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1888 deals with the actual denotation of Dishonour cheque and also imposes criminal liability upon a person who unknowingly/knowingly dishonors cheque. Back in 1988, through amendment, the civil wrong was transformed into an offence and thereby was criminalized. The amendment was based on the report on the committee on banking laws by Dr. Rajamannar, submitted in 1975, which suggested, inter alia, penalizing the act of dishonour. Cheque Dishonour followed by default in payment after a demand notice became punishable under Section 138 with imprisonment or fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or both.2

Key Ingredients of section 138

In Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan3, the court read Section 138 of the Act with section 177 to 179 of CrPC, 1973. It was observed that the offence under Section 138 can be completed only with the concatenation of the following ingredients:

Cheque should be issued to discharge any debt or liability, wholly or partly, through a live account.

Cheque should be presented within six months (now three months according to the latest directive of RBI) or before its validity expires.

The cheque issued should have been returned by the bank because of the insufficient amount of money in the drawer's account or exceeds the credit arrangement to the payee or holder by the bank itself.

The payee or holder within thirty days should have issued a notice to make a demand for the payment of the said amount since the bank returned the cheque unpaid.

The drawer of such cheque fails to make payment to the payee or holder in the due course, within 15 days from the receipt of that demand.

From the expiry of those 15 days, the payee or holder is allowed to file a complaint in writing, within a period of one month.

Reasons to decriminalise the dishonor of Cheque

Apart from the violation of international conventions, we are still using that mode of payment in which the majority of strong economies are now discouraging it and moving towards a less-cash society by opting for other better alternatives. The rationale behind decriminalising includes the following noteworthy points:

(1)

Unequal treatment among debtors – Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act bifurcates and discriminates, and provides different treatment to different debtors. For instance, if a millionaire company goes bankrupt in India, Directors take the shield of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and hence they are not sent to jail for taking the company into bankruptcy. Then why an individual, who commits the same offence, is booked with a criminal charge and sent to jail?4

(2)

Contravenes Contract Law – For instance, in cases of post-dated cheque, a party cannot unilaterally terminate the contract, even if the contract allows so, as there would always be a fear of initiation of a criminal proceeding for cheque bounce against them.

4. Legal Framework of the Dishonour of Cheque

(a) The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Sections 138 to 147 - To ensure promptitude and remedy against defaulters and to make sure credibility of the holders of the negotiable instrument, a criminal remedy of penalty was inserted in the Act, in form of the Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 that inserted sections 138 to 147 in the Act, which were further modified by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002.

The issue of dishonour of cheque is dealt with under sections 138 to 147 that provide for remedies and various forms of punishment in case of dishonour of cheque. Section 138 deals with the dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. It provides that a person shall be punishable for two years imprisonment or with fine, if the cheque issued by drawers is returned by the bank unpaid. The cheque must be issued in discharge of whole or part, of any debt or other liability.

The presumption in favour of holder is drawn against the drawer and in favour of the holder under section 13911 of the Act that cheque is received by the holder in discharge of whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Further, section 1401 2 of the Act provides that a person drawing a cheque cannot take up the defence that when he drew the cheque he had no idea that his credit balance in the account was insufficient.

The offences by the companies have been dealt with under section 1411 3 (1) of the Act, which provides that if a person committing an offence under the section is a company, every person who at the time when offence was committed, was in-charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

Section 14214 of the Act states that the cognizance of an offence can be taken under section 138 upon a complaint in writing which must be made within one month by the payee or holder in due course from the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138.15 If there is no proof of service of the notice of demand as required under section 138, the prosecution of the drawer is not permissible.16

The summary trial of cases has been provided under section 1431 7 of the Act. Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) (in short ‘code’), all offences under this Chapter shall be tried by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or by a Metropolitan Magistrate and the provisions of sections 262 to 265 of the Code shall, as far as may be, apply to such trials. Further, under section 14418 of the Act, mode of service of summons has been provided. Section 14519 deals with the evidence on affidavit. Section 14620 provides that bank’s slip is prima facie evidence of certain facts and section 14721 states that all the offences punishable under the Act shall be compoundable.

(b) Judicial Perspective on Dishonour of Cheque - The Supreme Court is also very strict to punish the persons who are liable for the dishonour of cheque when presented before the bank for the payment. Our judiciary has upheld the constitutional validity of the law, i.e., section 138.22

Introduction

Dishonour of cheques has now become a perennial issue that has led to docket explosion due to prolonged trials and perhaps inefficiency in timely disposal of the cases. In the recent past, cases involving the dishonour of cheques were observed to be languishing before the subordinate courts that even prompted the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India ("Supreme Court") to take suo motu cognizance of the prolonged and never-ending trials of cases filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 ("the Act")1. Whilst there are multiple grey areas that still require an authoritative decision from the apex court, the present article endeavors to shed light on a pressing issue i.e., the incoherent error committed by a learned trial court by selectively issuing summons to the authorized signatory of the cheque, without summoning the company on whose behalf the cheque was issued.

To illustrate in simpler terms, while taking cognizance of the complainant for dishonor of cheque issued on companies' behalf, if a trial court solely summons the signatory of the cheque and not the company and its directors in-charge as arrayed in the complaint, that creates an untoward legal anomaly, disadvantageous to the innocuous complainant. Anillogical approach of issuing summons to the signatory of the cheque, but not the company on whose behalf the cheque was issued, negates the scheme of the Act, jeopardizing the legitimate claims of the complainant and prejudicial to its right.

In cases of not arraying the Company as a respondent in a complaint filed for dishonour of the cheque issued on behalf of the Company, the Supreme Court in Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels & Tours (P.) Ltd.2, observed it to be a vital and substantial error, enabling ground for quashing of the complaint under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ("CrPC").

In view of the above background, the purported research question arises in cases where the company is arrayed as an accused along with other necessary parties i.e. signatory of cheque and director(s), however, the summons is exclusively issued to the signatory of the cheque but not to the company. Not issuing summons to the company by the Ld. Trial Court is an error which is fatal in nature for quashing complaint in its entirety or is it an error that can be rectified at the stage of trial is the moot proposition that warrants an answer.

The present article attempts to address the aforesaid question, to ascertain the resource available to the innocuous complainant, whose rights are at stake, due to the incoherent approach taken by the Ld. Trial Court. The failure of the learned trial courts in not issuing the summons to the accused company and only issuing summons to the authorized signatory has been a specific problem and thus prompted the authors to address the research and the practical nuances involved therein.

To avoid confusion, it must be noted that this article is not from the viewpoint whereby the complainant fails to make any averments against the accused company and its directors and also fails to array them as accused in the complaint. On the contrary, this research addresses the situation where the complainant has arraigned the company and all its directors as the accused, but the learned trial court has erred whilst issuing summons solely to the signatory of cheque and not to the Company.

To emphasize on the underlying issue, it is indispensable to firstly, address the relevant provisions of the Act; secondly, bring forward the solutions to the problem posed above in light of the judicial trends; and thirdly, conclude on the note that even errors by the trial court open the floodgate of litigation across all courts and perhaps even allow the accused to deploy mischievous tactics to impede a genuine case of the complainant.

Dishonour of cheques has now become a perennial issue that has led to docket explosion due to prolonged trials and perhaps inefficiency in timely disposal of the cases. In the recent past, cases involving the dishonour of cheques were observed to be languishing before the subordinate courts that even prompted the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India ("Supreme Court") to take suo motu cognizance of the prolonged and never-ending trials of cases filed under Section 138 of

An Overview of Section 138 under N.I. Act

Negotiable Instruments have long been used in the business world as one of the simplest ways to move capital. Until 1988, there was no effective legislative mechanism to prevent individuals from issuing checks without adequate funds in their account, nor was there any severe penalty for doing so. For instance, a legal responsibility arose from the non-payment of checks. To secure the check's drawee, it was decided that cheque dishonour should be considered a criminal offence. Banking, Public Financial Institutions, and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 added Sec.138 to 142 for that reason. This was accomplished by having the drawer responsible for fines if the check bounced due to a lack of funds, with sufficient protections in place to deter abuse of the truthful drawer. However, it was later discovered that the courts were unwilling to resolve the proceedings in a timely and efficient fashion. The loopholes were filled in by the amendment of 2002, which resulted in the passage of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The provisions of sections 143 to 147 were included, and the provisions of sections 138, 141, and 142 were changed.

This amendment act aimed to control the growing business, exchange, commerce, and industrial activities and encourage greater financial vigilance. Also, to protect creditors' trust in the cheque box. The Hon'ble SC in the matter of Modi Cements Ltd. v. Kuchil Kumar Nandi held that "The object of Chapter XVII, containing Sections 138 to 142, is to promote the efficacy of banking operations and to ensure credibility in transacting business through cheques."1

Under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there are presumptions in favour of the receiver of the cheque that it was drawn to discharge debts or liabilities. It is, however, rebuttable, and the victim will refute it by cross-examination without having to reach the witness box. The complainant is also responsible for proving that the check was given for a properly enforceable debt or liability. The burden on the accused in such a situation will be heavier than in proceedings under section 114 of the Evidence Act. The operation of notification is deemed to have been effected until notice is submitted by registered mail to the proper addressee of the cheque, as stated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The drawer, on the other hand, is free to refute this assumption as per N. Paraeswaran Unni v. G. Kannan2. Section 139 provides a requirement that the holder of a cheque collects the cheque in discharge, in full or in part, of any debt or other obligation until the execution of the cheque is admitted, It was held in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa3. Cheques with no date or post-dated cheques are often given. In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar4, the Supreme Court held that if a signed blank cheque is willingly handed over to a payee for any payment, the payee is free to fill in the balance and other information. This will not invalidate the check on its own.

In the case of Kusum Ingots and Alloys Ltd v. Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd5, the Supreme Court found out the basic ingredients of the crime as contemplated under Sec.138 of the act that, "an individual must have drawn a check on a bank account that he maintains for transfer of a certain sum of money to another person from that account for the discharge of some debt or other liability; the cheque was issued to the bank within six months of the date on which it was drawn, or within the validity limit of the cheque, whichever comes first; According to RBI guidelines, the validity duration of Cheques, Demand Drafts, Pay Orders, and Banker's Cheques has been shortened from six to three months as of April 1, 2012, from the date of the instrument. The bank returns the check as outstanding. either because the sum of money in the account is inadequate to honour the cheque or because it reaches the amount arranged to be charged by the account under a bank agreement; within 30 days of receiving details from the bank about the return of the cheque as outstanding, the payee or issuer of the cheque makes a case for reimbursement of the said sum of money by sending a note in writing to the drawer of the cheque; within 15 days of receiving the said note, the drawer of the cheque fails to allow delivery of the said sum of money to the payee or the holder of the cheque in the proper course of the cheque."

Summing up 7. According to section 138, where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him is returned by the Bank unpaid for reasons mentioned in said section, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence. The proviso to the section stipulates three conditions on the satisfaction of which, the offence is said to be completed. The proviso inter alia obliges the payee to make a demand for the payment of said amount of money by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque and if the drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount within 15 days of the receipt of said notice, the stages stipulated in the proviso stand fulfilled. The notice u/s. 138 is required to be given to the drawer of the cheque so as to give the drawer an opportunity to make the payment and escape the penal consequences. No other person is contemplated by section 138 as being entitled to be issued such notice. The plain language of section 138 is very clear and leaves no room for any doubt or ambiguity. There is nothing in section 138, which may even remotely suggest issuance of notice to anyone other than the drawer.

7.1 Section 141 stipulates that if the person committing an offence u/s. 138 is a company, every director of such company, who was in charge of and responsible to that company for conduct of its business, shall also be deemed to be guilty. The reason for creating vicarious liability is plainly that a juristic entity i.e. a company would be run by living persons, who are in charge of its affairs and who guide the actions of that company and that it such juristic entity is guilty, those, who were responsible for its affairs and who guided actions of such juristic entity, must be held responsible and ought to be proceeded against. Section 141 again does not lay down any requirement that in such eventuality, the directors must individually be issued separate notices u/s. 138. The persons, who are in charge of the affairs of the company and running its affairs must naturally be aware of the notice of demand u/s. 138 of the Act issued to such company. It is precisely for this reason that no notice is additionally contemplated to be given to such directors. The opportunity to the drawer company is considered good enough for those, who are in charge of the affairs of such company. If it is their case that the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they had exercised due diligence to prevent such commission, it would be a matter of defence to be considered at the appropriate stage in the trial and certainly not at the stage notice u/s. 138.

7.2 No requirement of notice to all the directors -

If the requirement that such individual notices to the directors must additionally be given is read into the concerned provisions, it will not only be against the plain meaning and construction of the provision but will make the remedy u/s. 138 wholly cumbersome. In a given case, the ordinary lapse or negligence on part of the company could easily be rectified and amends could be made upon receipt of a notice u/s. 138 by the company. It would be unnecessary at that point to issue notices to all the directors, whose names the payee may not even be aware of at that stage. Under second proviso to section 138, the notice of demand has to be made within 30 days of the dishonour of cheque and the third proviso gives 15 days time to the drawer to make the payment of the amount and escape the penal consequences. Under clause (a) of section 142, the complaint must be filed within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under the third proviso to section 138. Thus, a complaint can be filed within the aggregate period of 75 days from the dishonor, by which time a complainant can gather requisite information as regards names and other details as to who were in charge of and how they were responsible for the affairs of the company. But, if we accept the logic that has weighed with the HC in the present case, such period gets reduced to 30 days only. Furthermore, unlike proviso to clause (b) of section 142 of the Act, such period is non-extendable. The summary remedy created for the benefit of a drawee of a dishonoured cheque will thus, be rendered completely cumbersome and capable of getting frustrated.

6.3 Twin contingencies under section 138 to be interpreted strictly - The two contingencies mentioned in section 138 have to be interpreted 'strictly or literally'. The expression "amount of money…. is insufficient" in section 138 is a genus and dishonour for reasons such "as account closed", "payment stopped", "referred to the drawer" are only species of that genus. Just as dishonour of a cheque on the ground that the account has been closed is a dishonour falling in the first contingency referred to in section 138, so also dishonour on the ground that the "signatures do not match" or that the "image is not found", which too implies that the specimen signatures do not match the signatures on the cheque would constitute a dishonour within the meaning of section 138 of the Act. The Court has said that on the parity of the decision in the earlier cases where it has been held that if after issue of the cheque, the drawer closes the account then it must be presumed that the amount in the account was nil hence, insufficient to meet the demand of the cheque. A similar result can be brought about by the drawer changing his specimen signature given to the bank or in the case of a company, the company changing the mandate of those authorized to sign the cheques on its behalf. Such changes or alteration in the mandate may be dishonest or fraudulent and that would inevitably result in dishonour of all cheques signed by the previously authorized signatories. According to the Court, there is no qualitative difference between a situation where the dishonour takes place on account of the substitution by a new set of authorized signatories resulting in the dishonour of the cheques already issued and another situation in which the drawer of the cheque changes his signatures or closes the account or issues instructions to the bank not to make the payment. So long as the change is brought about with a view to preventing the cheque being honoured the dishonour would become an offence under section 138 subject to other conditions prescribed being satisfied. In situations where mismatch in signatures is inadvertent – never intended by the drawer or where the authorized signatory gets changed in the ordinary course of business of a company, the question whether or not there was a lawfully recoverable debt or liability for discharge whereof the cheque was issued would be a matter that the trial Court will examine, having regard to the evidence adduced before it and keeping in view the statutory presumption that unless rebutted the cheque is presumed to have been issued for a valid consideration.

The words "sufficient ground for proceeding" again suggest that ground should be made out in the complaint for proceeding against the respondent. It is settled law that at the time of issuing of the process the Magistrate is required to see only the allegations in the complaint and where allegations in the complaint or the charge sheet do not constitute an offence against a person, the complaint is liable to be dismissed. A perusal of the provisions of sections 291 to 293 of the Companies Act shows that what a board of directors is empowered to do in relation to a particular company depends upon the role and functions assigned to directors as per the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company. There is nothing which suggests that simply by being a director in a company, one is supposed to discharge particular functions on behalf of a company. It happens that a person may be a director in a company but he may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of the company. As a director, he may be attending meetings of the board of directors of the company where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. It may be that a board of directors may appoint sub-Committees consisting of one or two directors out of the board of the company who may be made responsible for day-to-day functions of the company. These are matters which form part of resolutions of board of directors of a company. Nothing is oral. What emerges from this is that the role of a director in a company is a question of fact depending on the peculiar facts in each case. There is no universal rule that a director of a company is in-charge of its everyday affairs. There is no magic as such in a particular word, be it director, manager or secretary. It all depends upon respective roles assigned to the officers in a company. When the requirement in section 141, which extends the liability to officers of a company, is that such a person should be in-charge of and responsible to the company for conduct of business of the company, a person cannot be subjected to liability of criminal prosecution without it being averred in the complaint that he satisfies those requirements. Not every person connected with a company is made liable under section 141. Liability is cast on persons who may have something to do with the transaction complained of. A person, who is in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of a company, would naturally know why the cheque in question was issued and why it got dishonoured.

The position of a Managing Director or a Joint Managing Director in a company may be different. These persons, as the designation of their office suggests, are in-charge of a company. In order to escape liability such persons may have to bring their case within meaning of the proviso to section 141(1), that is, they will have to prove that when the offence was committed they had no knowledge of the offence or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence.

While analyzing section 141, it will be seen that it operates in cases where an offence under section 138 is committed by a company. The key words which occur in the section are ‘every person’. These are general words and take every person connected with a company within their sweep. Therefore, these words have been rightly qualified by use of the words "who, at the time the offence was committed, was in-charge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence, etc." What is required is that the persons who are sought to be made criminally liable under section 141 should be at the time the offence was committed, in-charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company. Every person connected with the company shall not fall within the ambit of the provision. It is only those persons who were in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of the company at the time of commission of an offence, that they will be liable for criminal action. It follows from this that if a director of a company was not in-charge of and was not responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the relevant time, he will not be liable under the provision. The liability arises from being in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of the company at the relevant time when the offence was committed and not on the basis of merely holding a designation or office in a company. Conversely, a person not holding any office or designation in a company may be liable if he satisfies the main requirement of being in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of a company at the relevant time. Liability depends on the role one plays in the affairs of a company and not on designation or status. If being a Director or Manager or Secretary was enough to cast criminal liability, the section would have said so. Instead of ‘every person’ the section would have said ‘every Director, Manager or Secretary in a company is liable’ .....etc. The Legislature is aware that it is a case of criminal liability which means serious consequences so far as the person sought to be made liable is concerned. Therefore, only persons who can be said to be connected with the commission of a crime at the relevant time have been subjected to action.

Complainant/Payee has no onus to prove the financial capacity at the threshold.

In proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act, the Complainant is not required to establish their financial capacity at the initial stage. Once the drawer admits to signing the cheque, the statutory presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act operates in favour of the Complainant, presuming the existence of a legally enforceable debt. The onus is not on the Complainant at the threshold to prove their financial wherewithal to make the payment in discharge of which the cheque was allegedly issued. Only if an objection is specifically raised in the reply notice or any pleading that the Complainant lacked the financial position to advance the claimed loan amount, would the Complainant be required to bring cogent material indicating financial capacity and actual advancement of the loan.

Recently, in Ashok Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh25, the Appellant/Complainant had advanced a loan to the Accused, who in discharge of the debt, issued a cheque. When presented, the cheque was dishonoured with the endorsement "payment stopped by drawer." A legal notice was sent within, but the Accused neither replied nor made payment. The Trial Court and Appellate Court convicted the Accused under Section 138 of the NI Act after finding the debt legally enforceable. However, the High Court reversed this decision, holding that the Complainant failed to prove his case because he did not disclose bank account details, the date of withdrawal, or the specific date when the cheque was obtained. The Supreme Court found this approach fundamentally erroneous. The Accused had admitted signing the cheque but claimed it was lost, though the intimation about the lost cheque was suspiciously sent to the police only a year after the cheque was presented. Further, the Accused had not raised the defence of the Complainant's lack of financial capacity in his reply notice. In fact, no reply was given to the statutory notice at all.

2.2 Presumption in favour of the holder - Section 139 raises a presumption in favour of holder. Section 139 provides that unless the contrary is proved, the Court shall presume that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for the discharge (in whole or in part) of any debt or other liability. In order to constitute an offence under section 138, one of the essential ingredients is that the cheque must have been issued in discharge of debt or other liability. In a criminal case the burden of proof is on the complainant. By virtue of section 139, there is an initial presumption in favour of the complainant. Section 139 introduces an exception to the general rule as to the burden of proof and shifts the onus on the accused. It is a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. The presumption under Section 139 is a presumption of law, as distinguished from presumption of facts. The effect of this presumption is to place the evidential burden on the drawer of proving that the cheque was not received towards the discharge of any liability. The presumption under section 139 has to be applied only to cases referred to under section 138 of Act, which are cases of issuing cheque for discharge of any liability and dishonour thereof and in no other case.

Negotiable instrument passes from hand to hand on endorsement and it would make trading very difficult and negotiability of the instrument impossible, unless certain presumptions are made. The presumption, therefore, is a matter of principle to facilitate negotiability as well as trade. It is also a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation as the complainant will not have to prove the reason for issuance of cheque as it shall be presumed that the cheque was issued in discharge of debt or liability. Thus, in a case of dishonour of cheque, the Court shall presume that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for the discharge of any debt or other liability. The debt or liability may be discharged in whole or in part.

Mandate of the section - The Supreme Court in the case of Maruti Udyog Ltd. v. Narender, [1999] 1 SCC 113 held that in view of the express provision of section 139, a presumption must be drawn that the holder of the cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138, for the discharge of any debt or other liability unless the contrary is proved. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan [1999] 7 SCC 510 the Court held that section 139 of the Act enjoins on the Court to presume that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge of any debt or liability.

The Supreme Court in Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee [2001] 32 SCL 499 held that both Sections 138 and 139 require that the court "shall presume" the liability of the drawer of the cheques for the amounts for which the cheques are drawn. It is obligatory on the court to raise this presumption in every case where the factual basis for the raising of the presumption had been established.

In other words, provided the facts required to form the basis of a presumption of law exist, no discretion is left with the court but to draw the statutory conclusion, but this does not preclude the person against whom the presumption is drawn from rebutting it and proving the contrary.

Rebuttable Presumption – it is pertinent to note that the presumption mandated under section 139 is a rebuttable presumption. The accused can show that the cheques were not issued in discharge of any debt or liability. The Supreme Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan [2010] 100 SCL 389 also held that the presumption under section 139 is in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested.

Evidence in case of rebuttal – In order to rebut the presumption, the accused may either adduce direct evidence or adduce circumstantial evidence to prove that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. The Court need not insist that direct evidence be produced in every case.

The Supreme Court of India in the case of SampellySatyanarayan Rao V Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd [2016] 74 taxmann.com 68/138 SCL 73 held that dishonour of post dated cheques issued for discharge of existing liability (though given as security) shall be covered under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. This Article highlights the circumstances under which a person is liable for dishonour of post date cheque with comparison with other judgments of the Supreme Court on the same.

Introduction

1. If a drawer of a cheque issues a cheque for consideration and if it is dishonoured then he is liable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. In other words, the drawer of the cheque is liable for debt or other liability which is legally enforceable debt or other liability and not for dishonour of cheque given for security of the total loan. Usually, the cheque for repayment of the loan will be given as a post dated cheque as "security". This means that the drawer of the cheque is liable even for dishonour of the cheque given for security if on the date of the cheque liability or debt exists or the amount has become legally recoverable. This article highlights the fact that the Supreme Court in the case of Sampelly Satyanarayan Rao v. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd, [2016] 74 taxmann.com 68/138 SCL 73 has given the judgment that dishonour of post dated cheques issued for discharge of existing liability shall be covered by the Negotiable Instruments Act.

Provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act

Introduction:

The term Negotiable instrument has been used in the world commercially for a very long period since it was one of the most convenient modes of transferring monetary assets. Before 1988 there was no legal provision that was quite effective to restrain the people from issuing cheques without having enough amount to transfer or any stringent provision to punish them. As we know, on dishonouring of cheques, civil legal liability arises. Thus, considering this point, the legislature came up with the provision which helps the drawee of the cheque who is facing such problem, punishable offences can be issued for this. For this section 138 to 142 was inserted by Negotiable Instrument Law (Amendments). All these efforts were made for making the drawer liable for all the penalties in case of bouncing of cheques. However, in recent times it has been seen that the courts are unable to dispose off the case in a time-bound manner. Many loopholes were rectified by the various amendments in the year 2002 and thus, the Negotiable Instrument Act 2002 was passed. The provisions of section 143 to 147 were newly inserted and various amendments were made. The major objective of the amendments was first to regulate the growing businesses, trades and industrial activities. Secondly, to promote vigilance in financial matters. Thirdly, to protect the trust of the creditors in the drawer cheques. The Apex court in the Modi Cement Case1 observed that the objective of the making of chapter XVII, Containing sections 138 to 142, is to promote the efficiency of banking operation and to ensure transferring of cheques could be made without any fraud.

Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act:

This article focuses on section 138, and the section 13 of this act defines Negotiable Instrument as a promissory note, cheque payable either to order or to the bearer and also bills of exchange i.e. a Negotiable Instrument is a document that assures the beneficiary an amount of money which is payable on the demand or in future. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act provides a provision in which it deals with all the violations of dishonour of cheques. Dishonouring of cheques is not an offence in itself but in order to be considered as an offence, the following mentioned points must be present:

-

There should be a drawer that draws the cheque

-

The cheque which is to be drawn should carry some purpose

-

A cheque should be presented in the drawee bank

-

The cheque which is returned by the bank should carry the reason of insufficient amount

-

The cheque should be presented before the bank within six months from the date mentioned on the cheque

-

The memo should be returned to the bank within 30 days' notice should be provided to the demand of payment of the said amount

-

The drawer should have failed to pay the said amount within 15 days of the notice

Vicarious liability

Vicarious mean acting or done for another. A person is vicariously liable for the act done by another.

Since a legal person is a fiction of the law and does not exist in actuality, the issue of vicarious liability of the office bearers through whom a company, or a partnership or association of persons must necessarily act, comes to the fore. Many modern statutes incorporates stringent principle of strict vicarious criminal liability of persons who are responsible to the company or firm or association of persons for the conduct of its business or are its responsible office bearers like the director, manager, secretary in particular or the member of association. Strict vicarious liability is somewhat an exception to the general rule of direct personal culpability and is a modern development through statutory provisions. That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principle of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept wholeheartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either the aforesaid ingredients.

Vicarious liability "is a necessary doctrine for the proper enforcement of much modern legislation - but is not one to be extended" [Gardner v. Akeroyd (1952) 2 QB 743]. The normal rule against vicarious liability in cases involving criminal liability that no one is to be held criminally liable for an act of another, is subject to exception on account of specific provision being made in statutes extending liability to others [S.M.S Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla [2005] 127 Comp. Cas. 563 (SC)]. The Supreme Court in that case observed that section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is an instance to a specific provision which in case an offence under section 138 of the Act is committed by a company, extends criminal liability for dishonour of a cheque to officers of the company and that since the provision creates criminal liability, the conditions which have to be satisfied before the liability can be extended to officers of a company have to be strictly complied with. The conditions are intended to ensure that a person who is sought to be made vicariously liable for an office of which the principal accused is the company, had a role to play in relation to the incriminating act and further that such a person should know what is attributed to him to make him liable. In other words, persons who had nothing to do with the matter need not be roped in.

Whether one person will be held responsible for the acts of another is a matter of construction in each case. Regard must be had to the object of the statute, the words used, the nature of the duty laid down, the person upon whom it is imposed, the person by whom it would in ordinary circumstances be performed and the person upon whom the penalty is imposed [Mousell Bros. Ltd. v. L.M.W. Rly. Co. (1917) 2 KB 836]

If the doctrine of vicarious liability is held to apply, a person subject to a statutory duty to which a penal sanction is attached who chooses to delegate the performance of that duty to another person (usually but not necessarily an employee), will nevertheless be himself liable for breaches of that duty by his delegate. In many cases his delegate’s ‘knowledge’ will be imputed to him [see Vane v. Vianmopoullos (1965) AC 486 and Gifford v. Police (1965) NZLR 484]

De Rutzen [1895] 1 QB 918 Wright, J., found that there are three classes of cases where the Legislature normally enacts absolute prohibition : (1) One is a class of acts which, in the language of Lush J. in Davis v. Harvey (Law Rep. 9 QB 433) are not criminal in any real sense, but are acts which in the public interest are prohibited under a penalty. Several such instances are to be found in the decisions on the Revenue Statutes, Adulteration Acts, Games Acts etc.;

(2) Another class comprehends some, and perhaps all, public nuisances : Reg v. Stephens (Law Rep 1 QB 702) where the employer was held liable on the indictment for a nuisance caused by workmen without his knowledge and contrary to his orders;

(3) Lastly, there may be cases in which, although the proceeding is criminal in form, it is really a summary mode of enforcing a civil right : see per Williams and Willes JJ. in Modern v. Porter [7 C.B (N.S.) 641; 29 LJ (M.C. 213], as to the unintentional trespass in pursuit of game; Lee v. Simpson (3 C.B. 871) as to unconscious dramatic piracy and Hargreaves v. Diddams (Law Rep. 10 QB 582), as to a bona fide belief in a legally impossible right to fish.

In the case of absolute liability where the Legislature by the clearest intendment establishes an offence where liability arises instantly upon the breach of the statutory prohibition, no particular state of mind is a prerequisite to guilt. Corporations and individual persons stand on the same footing in the face of such a statutory offence. It is a case of automatic primary responsibility. It is only in a case requiring mens rea, a question arises whether a corporation could be attributed with requisite mens rea to prove the guilt." A company is capable of criminal intention [see Director of Public Prosecutions v. Kent & Sussex Contractors Ltd. [1944] 4 Comp. Cas. 133 (DC)]. It can be indicted for an offence of conspiracy to defraud [see R v. ICR Haulage Ltd. [1945] 15 Comp. Cas. 47 (CA)]. A company cannot be guilty of any criminal offence, which by their nature, can only be committed by natural persons (such as bigamy). Nor of those which cannot be committed vicariously (such as perjury, bigamy, rape, homicide, etc. (see State of Maharashtra v. Syndicate Transport Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1964 Bom. 195). It cannot also be indicted for a crime where the only punishment is death or imprisonment (see Rex v. ICR Haulage (1944) 1 All ER 691). Kenny in the Outlines of Criminal Law (The Outlines of Criminal law by Kenny, 15th edition at pages 73 to 75) observes as under :

‘Moreover a corporation is devoid not only of mind, but also of body; and therefore incapable of the usual criminal punishments. "Can you hang its common seal?" asked an advocate in James KK’s days (8 St. Tr. 1138).

Thus the fact that a corporation cannot be hanged or imprisoned sets a limit to the range of criminal liability. A corporation can only be prosecuted, as such, for offences which can be punished by a fine.’

As a company cannot be sentenced to imprisonment, that court cannot impose that punishment. But when imprisonment and fine is the prescribed punishment, the court can impose the punishment of fine which can be enforced against the company [see Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 275 ITR 81 (SC)]

A company may be guilty both of statutory and common law offences (of course in exceptional cases in respect of common law offences), even though the latter involves mens rea. A corporation can be indicted for contempt and libel.

Fixed deposit - Joint account

A fixed deposit in the joint names of two persons is nothing but a joint account which, as the name itself suggests, is payable on the expiration of the agreed period. The fixed deposit receipt is merely a written acknowledgement by the bank that it holds a certain sum to the use of its customers. The bank is thus a debtor to the account holders in respect of the amount deposited a debt which is repayable by the bank to the account holder with interest on the expiry of an agreed period. [Anumati v. Punjab National Bank [2005] 126 Comp. Cas. 322 (SC)]

It has to be established that at the time offence was committed, the director was in-charge of and was responsible to company for conduct of business of company - Shailendra Swarup v. Deputy Director, Enforcement (2020) 161 SCL 1 = 118 taxmann.com 9 (SC). In VBC Exports v. Commander S D Baijal (1996) 5 SCC 382 = (1998) 91 Comp Cas 63 (SC), the managing director was found to be responsible for conduct of business of the company. He was held guilty as he did not bring on record any material to show that offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised due diligence to prevent its commission. It was held that burden is on him to prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or that he took due diligence to prevent commission of the offence.

18.17-3 Directors etc. liable only if offense committed with their connivance or due to their negligence

As per clause (2) of the section (as contained in many of the Acts), in case of other directors, manager and Secretary, they are held guilty only when it is proved that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or is attributable to their negligence, i.e. the burden of proof is on prosecution (complainant) to allege and prove that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or negligence.

In SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla (2005) 8 SCC 89 = 148 Taxman 128 = 63 SCL 93 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that simply being a director in a company, one is not supposed to be in-charge of affairs of the company. A director may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of a company. As a director, he may be attending meetings of Board where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. One or two directors may be made responsible for day-to-day functions of the company by a resolution. - - However, in case of MD or JMD, by virtue of the office they hold as Managing Director or Joint Managing Director, these persons are in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. In order to escape liability, they have to prove that when the offense was committed, they had no knowledge of the offense or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent commission of the offense [decision in case of bouncing of cheque under Negotiable Instruments Act, but principle should apply in all cases].

It is trite law that wherever a legal fiction of the principle of vicarious liability is attracted, and a person otherwise not personally involved in the commission of an offense is made liable for the same, it has to be specifically provided in the statute concerned - Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Datar Switchgear Ltd. (2010) 10 SCC 479 = 105 SCL 253 = 8 taxmann.com 223 = 159 Comp Cas 545 (SC).

In State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal (1998) 93 Comp Cas 329 (SC) = (1998) 5 SCC 343 = AIR 1998 SC 2327 = 1998 AIR SCW 2240, (matter under Drugs & Cosmetics Act), it was held that vicarious liability of a person for an offence of company arises only if at the material time he was in charge of and was also responsible to the company for conduct of its business. Simply because a person is a director does not mean that both these requirements are fulfilled. If there is not even allegation that the director was in charge and responsible to the company, he cannot be prosecuted. - following Delhi Municipal Corporation v. Ram Kishan Rothgi (1983) 1 SCC 1 = AIR 1983 SC 67. - same view in Shyam Sunder v. State of Haryana AIR 1989 SC 1982 = (1989) 4 SCC 630 = 67 Comp Cas 1 (SC), where it was held that all directors cannot be held responsible. - followed in D G Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H), where in a case under Insecticides Act, it was held that complaint should state that the director was in charge and responsible to company - same view in Pepsico India Holdings P Ltd. v. Food Inspector (2011) 1 SCC 176 (SC 3 member bench).

In Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that director can be held vicariously liable only if (a) there is sufficient incriminating evidence against him coupled with criminal intent or (b) statutory regime attracts doctrine of vicarious liability.

Punishment for offences

The SARFAESI Act provides a general punishment of imprisonment upto one year or with fine, if any person contravenes or attempts to contravene any provision of Act. [section 29 of SARFAESI Act].

Cognizance of offence can be taken only upon complaint made by an officer of Central Registry or officer of RBI duly authorized for this purpose [section 30(1) of SARFAESI Act].

The penalty can be imposed by Court not lower that Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of First Class. [section 30(2) of SARFAESI Act].

4.5-1 Offences by company

If offence is committed by a company (the term includes partnership firm or association of individuals), every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 33(1) of SARFAESI Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 33(2) of SARFAESI Act].

Difference between provisions of section 33(1) and 33(2) of SARFAESI Act is that in former case, the person-in-charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

In Girdhari Lal Gupta v. D N Mehta AIR 1972 SC 2162, it was held that the first part of definition is applicable to the one who is in overall control of the company. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi AIR 1983 SC 67, it was held that there should be averment that director was responsible to the conduct of business of the company. Otherwise, he cannot be prosecuted - followed in D K Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H).

A director/partner as well as the Company/firm can be prosecuted. Of course, Company/firm can only be fined, while the guilty officers/partners can be imprisoned and personal fine also can be imposed. In some cases, it has been held that a director can be prosecuted even if company itself is not prosecuted.

Culpability of company under Income-tax Act/Wealth-tax Act 11.10-9 What should be disturbing indeed is the retrograde lead taken by the law-makers, to the relief of the Prosecutors and the Judiciary alike though, so far as the Income Tax Act and the Wealth Tax Act are concerned: a sub-section (3) has been added to sections 278B and 35HA, respectively, that came into force from 1st October, 2004, by the Finance Act (No.2) 2004, reading-"Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a person, being a company, and the punishment for such offence is imprisonment and fine, then, without prejudice to the provisions in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), such company shall be punished with fine and every person referred to in sub-section (1) or the director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company referred to in sub-section (2), shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished in accordance with the provisions of the Act". From the point of accountability of companies to the society at large with their great resource-backed potential for mischief it is unfortunate, the trend set in law of attribution of culpability to the company as such in our country is just to let it go with fine and nothing more to it. This development seems to be the result of the majority decision of the three member bench in Asstt. Commissioner v. Velliappa Textiles 2003 AIR SCW 5647, saying that a company cannot be prosecuted if the provision in law is punishment by imprisonment only. It is unfortunate because even in the present day modern social order it is difficult to assume that the King can do no wrong or that all of His wrongs are off in a money-wash, and a company and its directors being far less privileged than a King at any rate, some other alternative provision in law, may be business inhibitory in nature and commensurate to the seriousness of the economic offence involved at least for a short run of time, ought to be attributable to the company that stigmatises the directors automatically, in the interest of natural justice to curb the obsession with public mischief for private profit in disguise.

11.10-9a The trend has been stalled by Supreme Court - However, the later decision of Supreme Court in Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 275 ITR 81/145 Taxman 154 to the effect that there is no immunity to the companies from prosecution merely because the prosecution is in respect of offences for which the punishment prescribed is mandatory imprisonment, seems to be rational and correct, both in itself and constitutionally.

Background of ‘Standard Chartered’ majority verdict

11.10-10 The 2:1 decision of the three Judge Bench in Velliappa’s case is said to be in line with the Law Commission recommendation made in its 41st and 47th Reports suggesting amendments to the Acts relating to economic offences and the IPC to say that offences punishable with only imprisonment or imprisonment and fine means only fine when the offender is a company or corporation, leading to an amendment proposed to the IPC in 1972 that had lapsed. The majority decision in Velliappa’s case was based on the Act provision being mandatory imprisonment plus fine, leaving no choice to the Court to impose only fine in lieu of imprisonment, leading to the conclusion that a company cannot be prosecuted for such offences until the Act is amended as was done in Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Netherlands and the EU, on the footing that it is not Court’s function "to repair the blunders that are to be found in legislation. They must be corrected by the Legislature": Bristol Guardians v. Bristol Waterworks Co. (1914) AC 379. The minority judgment given by Mathur J. in the said case was that the Court would be shrinking from its responsibility of imparting justice by the conclusion that a juristic person like a company cannot be sent to jail and therefore it is free from prosecution even for serious offences which only attract mandatory imprisonment in law. The verdict of the 3-Judge Bench in ANZ Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 58 SCL 350 (SC) doubted the correctness of the majority verdict in Velliappa’s case; and in Standard Chartered case, cited above, a 5-Judge Bench gave the verdict with 3:2 majority that companies or corporations cannot go scot-free having committed serious offences, and it also cannot be the intention of the Legislature to grant blanket immunity in that fashion, and in that view of the matter it was taken that discretion is given to the Court to impose prison sentence or fine in such cases, over-ruling the Velliappa precedent.

by the master. The driver of a car taking the car on the masters’ business makes him vicariously liable if he commits an accident. But it is equally well-settled that if the servant, at the time of the accident, is not acting within the course of his employment, but is doing something for himself, the master is not liable. There is a presumption that a vehicle is driven on the master’s business and by his authorised agent or servant but presumption can be met.4 The owner would be liable for the acts done by his servant in the course of his employment vicariously but the liability of the owner would not extend to any criminal acts done by the servant,5 unless the criminal act of the servant is within the general scope of the servant’s employment.6 For an employer to be liable, however, it is not enough that the employment merely afforded the servant or agent an opportunity of committing the crime. It must be shown that the damage complained of is caused by any wrongful act of his servant or agent done within the scope or course of the servants’ or agents’ employment even if the wrongful act amounted to a crime.

5.22D-7j FRAUD BY SERVANT, MASTER IS LIABLE - A master is liable for his servant’s fraud perpetrated in the course of master’s business, whether the fraud is for the master’s benefit or not, if it is committed by servant in the course of his employment. There is no difference in the liability of a master for wrongs whether for fraud or any other wrong committed by servant in the course of employment, and it is a question of fact in each case, whether it is committed in the course of the employment.

5.22D-7k MENS REA IN CASE OF CRIMES COMMITTED BY COMPANIES - Though the company is a legal personality of its own, it cannot act in its own person. It must act through the agency of human beings. A corporation is an abstraction. It has no mind of its own any more than it has a body of its own; its active and directive will must consequently be sought in the person of somebody who for some purposes may be called an agent, but who is really the directing mind and will of the corporation, the very ego and centre of the personality of the corporation.

A corporation could not be subjected to bodily punishment. It could, however, be fined; and to this day fine remains the only mode of punishment applicable to a corporation. Since fine only is the type of punishment appropriate to a corporation, a corporation cannot be convicted of it, if a crime is not punishable with fine. The acts of the organs of the corporation are attributed to the corporation and treated for legal purposes as though they were acts of the corporation itself. However, when will an act or mental strain be imputed to a company as its own, is a question that has to be considered by a court, depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. A company can commit crimes only by its agents who must themselves be responsible for the crime, and it is a question in each case whether the act of the agent, including his state of mind, intention, knowledge or belief can be imputed to the corporation. It depends upon the nature of the charge, the position of the officer or agent relative to the corporation and other relevant facts and circumstances of the case. A company cannot be guilty of any criminal offence, which by its very nature, can only be committed by natural persons (such as bigamy). Nor of those which cannot be committed vicariously (such as perjury, bigamy, rape, homicide, etc.)1. A company cannot be indicted for a crime where the only punishment is death or imprisonment.2 A company may be guilty both of statutory and common law offences (of course in exceptional cases in respect of common law offences), even though the latter involves mens rea. A corporation can be indicted for contempt and libel.

Wherever a duty is imposed by statute in such a way that a breach of the duty amounts to disobedience of the law, then, if there is nothing in the statute either expressly or impliedly to the contrary, the breach of the statute is an offence for which a corporation will be indicted, whether or not the statute refers in terms to corporations.

A statute which creates a criminal offence may expressly or by necessary implications define the particular state of mind which is an element of offence or it may be silent on this point. It is of utmost importance to the protection of the liberty of the subject and of the corporation or company to which such state of mind is imputed by fiction that a Court shall always bear in mind that unless a statute either clearly or by necessary implication rules out mens rea as a constituent part of a crime, the court should not find a man guilty of an offence unless that person has a guilty mind. This principle will apply to the corporations also.1

The rigour and stringency of the rule is tempered by holding that such a person on whom the vicarious liability has been thrust may cast off such a liability if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. The burden of proof is clearly laid upon such a person and such is the rule of evidence which reverses the ordinary mandate of criminal liability that the burden of establishing the prosecution lies on the prosecution.

The rigour and stringency of the rule is tempered by holding that such a person on whom the vicarious liability has been thrust may cast off such a liability if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. The burden of proof is clearly laid upon such a person and such is the rule of evidence which reverses the ordinary mandate of criminal liability that the burden of establishing the prosecution lies on the prosecution. 5.22D-7l MENS REA IN RESPECT OF IMPUTED LIABILITY - Criminal liability could be an imputed liability as is found in section 278B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 or in a provision of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Industrial Disputes Act, Essential Commodities Act, 1955 etc. The liability is to be imputed to high managerial officers (who at the time of the commission of offence, were in charge of and responsible to the conduct of the company’s business), because the company cannot be executed or punished with corporal punishment. The person is liable because his action is the very action of the company itself and is charged as a person-in-charge of and responsible to the conduct of the company’s business, and not in his individual capacity. The prosecution case cannot rest on the ground that the person concerned is personally responsible for the commission or omission of the act. The prosecution has to be foisted upon him because he has been in charge of and responsible to the conduct of the business of the company. The person is not said to be prosecuted independently of his character as being the person-in-charge and responsible. Thus, once it is found that there had been contravention of the provisions of a statute by a company or a firm, the persons who are in charge of the business and are responsible for its conduct cannot escape liability, unless they prove by leading evidence that contravention took place without their knowledge or in spite of diligence exercised by them.2

The person ‘in charge’ must mean that the person should be in overall control of the day-to-day business of the company.3 The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Pratap Chand4 considered the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The three respondents being the partners of the firm, Mafatlal & Co., and the firm itself was charged for offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate found respondents 1 and 3, that is, one of the partners of the firm, guilty under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and sentenced respondent 1 to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500; in default, to suffer simple imprisonment for three months. Respondent 2 was acquitted of these two offences as the Magistrate found respondent 1 and not respondent 2 to be in charge of the business of the firm. All the respondents were acquitted of the offence. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court of Karnataka from the order of acquittal of respondent 2 of the offence.The High Court summarily dismissed the appeal. The partner of a firm is also liable under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act to be convicted for an offence committed by the firm if he was in charge of and responsible to the firm for the conduct of the business of the firm or if it is proved that the offence was committed with the consent or connivance of, or was attributable to any neglect on the part of the partner concerned. In the present case, respondent 2 was sought to be made liable on the ground that he along with the first respondent was in charge of the conduct of the business of the firm. Since it was found that respondent 1 and not respondent 2 was in overall control of day-to-day business of the firm, respondent 2 was held not liable to be convicted merely because he had the right to participate in the business of the firm under the terms of the partnership deed. In another case, Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana1, the Supreme Court held that there was no evidence that all the partners were conducting the business of the firm and, thus, all cannot be indicted for the offence under section 10 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The argument that in a firm each partner is a representative of the other was rejected by holding that it is relevant in a civil liability and not in criminal liability and that there is no vicarious liability in criminal law unless the statute takes that also within its fold.

The person who is liable to be proceeded and punished for imputed liabilities should be the one who was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the company’s business at the time of commission of the offence. The managing director of the company from his very designation implies both the control and command of the affairs of such a company and equally a statutory liability to the company for responsible conduct of its business. It is a compendious term which signifies both control of and responsibility to the company both in ordinary parlance and by virtue of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act. Similarly, in the case of manager, from the very nature of his duties, it can be safely inferred that he would undoubtedly by vicariously liable for the offences, vicarious liability being an incident of an offence.2

Where in a complaint, accused were not shown as "officer in default" they could not be held responsible merely because they were directors [see Ramesh Chandra Manilal Kotla v. State of Gujarat (1998) 30 CLA 313 (Guj.). In Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana [1990] 67 Comp. Cas. 1], the Supreme Court observed that all the partners of a firm are not liable for an offence committed by the firm irrespective of whether they were running the business or not, and it would be travesty of justice prosecute all the partners and ask them to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge. The obligation on the accused to prove that the offence took place without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent such offence arises only when the prosecution establishes that the requisite conditions mentioned in the relevant section is established. The ratio of the case is applicable in the case of a company also. A director who was neither a managing or whole-time director nor was involved in day-to-day affairs of the company cannot be said to be an officer in default [see H. Nanjundiah v. Govindan, Registrar of Companies [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 356 (Bom.)].

Possession involves animus and corpus.
