But it is equally well-settled that if the servant, at the time of the accident, is not acting within the course of his employment, but is doing something for himself, the master is not liable. There is a presumption that a vehicle is driven on the master’s business and by his authorised agent or servant but presumption can be met.4 The owner would be liable for the acts done by his servant in the course of his employment vicariously but the liability of the owner would not extend to any criminal acts done by the servant,5 unless the criminal act of the servant is within the general scope of the servant’s employment.6 For an employer to be liable, however, it is not enough that the employment merely afforded the servant or agent an opportunity of committing the crime. It must be shown that the damage complained of is caused by any wrongful act of his servant or agent done within the scope or course of the servants’ or agents’ employment even if the wrongful act amounted to a crime.

5.22D-7j FRAUD BY SERVANT, MASTER IS LIABLE - A master is liable for his servant’s fraud perpetrated in the course of master’s business, whether the fraud is for the master’s benefit or not, if it is committed by servant in the course of his employment. There is no difference in the liability of a master for wrongs whether for fraud or any other wrong committed by servant in the course of employment, and it is a question of fact in each case, whether it is committed in the course of the employment.

5.22D-7k MENS REA IN CASE OF CRIMES COMMITTED BY COMPANIES - Though the company is a legal personality of its own, it cannot act in its own person. It must act through the agency of human beings. A corporation is an abstraction. It has no mind of its own any more than it has a body of its own; its active and directive will must consequently be sought in the person of somebody who for some purposes may be called an agent, but who is really the directing mind and will of the corporation, the very ego and centre of the personality of the corporation.

A corporation could not be subjected to bodily punishment. It could, however, be fined; and to this day fine remains the only mode of punishment applicable to a corporation. Since fine only is the type of punishment appropriate to a corporation, a corporation cannot be convicted of it, if a crime is not punishable with fine. The acts of the organs of the corporation are attributed to the corporation and treated for legal purposes as though they were acts of the corporation itself. However, when will an act or mental strain be imputed to a company as its own, is a question that has to be considered by a court, depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. A company can commit crimes only by its agents who must themselves be responsible for the crime, and it is a question in each case whether the act of the agent, including his state of mind, intention, knowledge or belief can be imputed to the corporation. It depends upon the nature of the charge, the position of the officer or agent relative to the corporation and other relevant facts and circumstances of the case. A company cannot be guilty of any criminal offence, which by its very nature, can only be committed by natural persons (such as bigamy). Nor of those which cannot be committed vicariously (such as perjury, bigamy, rape, homicide, etc.)1. A company cannot be indicted for a crime where the only punishment is death or imprisonment.2 A company may be guilty both of statutory and common law offences (of course in exceptional cases in respect of common law offences), even though the latter involves mens rea. A corporation can be indicted for contempt and libel.

Wherever a duty is imposed by statute in such a way that a breach of the duty amounts to disobedience of the law, then, if there is nothing in the statute either expressly or impliedly to the contrary, the breach of the statute is an offence for which a corporation will be indicted, whether or not the statute refers in terms to corporations.

A statute which creates a criminal offence may expressly or by necessary implications define the particular state of mind which is an element of offence or it may be silent on this point. It is of utmost importance to the protection of the liberty of the subject and of the corporation or company to which such state of mind is imputed by fiction that a Court shall always bear in mind that unless a statute either clearly or by necessary implication rules out mens rea as a constituent part of a crime, the court should not find a man guilty of an offence unless that person has a guilty mind. This principle will apply to the corporations also.1

The rigour and stringency of the rule is tempered by holding that such a person on whom the vicarious liability has been thrust may cast off such a liability if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. The burden of proof is clearly laid upon such a person and such is the rule of evidence which reverses the ordinary mandate of criminal liability that the burden of establishing the prosecution lies on the prosecution.

4.5

Punishment for offences

The SARFAESI Act provides a general punishment of imprisonment upto one year or with fine, if any person contravenes or attempts to contravene any provision of Act. [section 29 of SARFAESI Act].

Cognizance of offence can be taken only upon complaint made by an officer of Central Registry or officer of RBI duly authorized for this purpose [section 30(1) of SARFAESI Act].

The penalty can be imposed by Court not lower that Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of First Class. [section 30(2) of SARFAESI Act].

4.5-1 Offences by company

If offence is committed by a company (the term includes partnership firm or association of individuals), every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 33(1) of SARFAESI Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 33(2) of SARFAESI Act].

Difference between provisions of section 33(1) and 33(2) of SARFAESI Act is that in former case, the person-in-charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

In Girdhari Lal Gupta v. D N Mehta AIR 1972 SC 2162, it was held that the first part of definition is applicable to the one who is in overall control of the company. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi AIR 1983 SC 67, it was held that there should be averment that director was responsible to the conduct of business of the company. Otherwise, he cannot be prosecuted - followed in D K Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H).

A director/partner as well as the Company/firm can be prosecuted. Of course, Company/firm can only be fined, while the guilty officers/partners can be imprisoned and personal fine also can be imposed. In some cases, it has been held that a director can be prosecuted even if company itself is not prosecuted.

As consequence of search conducted at the assessee's premises as well as those of his wife, FDR's and NSC's were seized from wife's premises as well as from locker with bank. Even the Court had noted the fact that the assessee and the wife were living separately since 10-10-1979. Thus, the whole case of the Assessing Officer was based on suspicion, surmises and conjectures and he had made additions in respect of assets found from the premises of the wife and from locker held by her and additions could not be sustained in law. - Asstt. Stridhan to husband - Entrustment of the stridhan by wife to husband cannot amount to a partnership between them [Pratibha Rani v. Suraj Kumar [1985] 155 ITR 190 (SC)].

Two separate partnerships having same partners - Each partnership agreement may constitute a distinct and separate partnership and, therefore, distinct and separate firms. That is not to say that a firm is a corporate entity or enjoys a juristic personality in that sense. The firm name is only a collective name for the individual partners. But each partnership is a distinct relationship. The partners may be different and yet the nature of the business may be the same, the businesses may be different and yet the partners may be the same. An agreement between the partners to carry on a business and share its profits may be followed by a separate agreement between the same partners to carry on another business and share the profits therein. The intention may be to constitute two separate partnerships and, therefore, two distinct firms or to extend merely a partnership originally constituted to carry on one business, to the carrying on of another business. It will all depend on the intention of the partners. The intention of the partners will have to be decided with reference to the terms of the agreement and all the surrounding circumstances, including evidence as to the interlacing or interlocking of management, finance and other incidents of the respective businesses [Deputy CST v. K. Kelukutty [1985] 22 Taxman 25 (SC)].

Cas. 16 (DB) (Bom.), it can be seen that the mental state of those in control and/or management of the company is attributable to the company itself as its "directing mind and will", to render the company indictable of their criminal acts in conducting the company’s business provided their criminal acts fall within the limits of their authority and proved as a matter of fact. At the same time, it has to be borne in mind what the Court had observed in the case cited to the effect that where there was a breach of an assurance or undertaking by a company, a criminal complaint filed against it under the Indian Penal Code was to be quashed as being abuse of power of the Court. However, there is as yet no authority of a decided case taking this development further forward to its logical conclusion laying down the rules of such attribution to the company for certain by the Courts generally whether under the Act or other economic legislation in particular. The present position seems to be that even in cases where the direct doer, agent or employee acting for it is caught in the act considered as an offence or a crime without mens rea, there is no way to attribute it to the company otherwise than by adducing evidence, which it is difficult to succeed. 11.10-5c-1 OFFENCES BY COMPANIES UNDER COMPANIES ACT - So far as the Com-panies Act, 1956 is concerned, the Act is not a complete code of all offences, but it carries several defaults but not offences mentioned in various sections for which the company is made directly liable to be penalized subject to compounding and fined with no irremovable stigma attaching except disallowance of the fine paid in income-tax assessment as a business expense resulting in incidence of tax on the fine, with nothing more needed for the Court to enquire in order to impose the penalties and fines pre-fixed in the sections. As regards the offences against the Act, it is only the concerned officers in default in addition who may be directly or deemed to be liable to the same and be imprisoned too. Again, only those persons are liable as are covered by section 5 of the Act giving the definition of ‘officer-in-default’ to be proceeded against in respect of several offences figuring in the Act (for a discussion on ‘officer-in-default’ see Chapter 18).

11.10-5d As regards crimes under IPC companies enjoy immunity - In respect of offences amounting to crimes against persons and property under the Indian Penal Code in which companies are involved, there is no manner established for attributing the criminality to the companies, and this forms a shield of impunity militating against proper administration of law and justice in corporate affairs, as can be seen from the decision in Naguneri Peace Memorial Co-operative Urban Bank Ltd. v. Culpability of company under Income-tax Act/Wealth-tax Act 11.10-9 What should be disturbing indeed is the retrograde lead taken by the law-makers, to the relief of the Prosecutors and the Judiciary alike though, so far as the Income Tax Act and the Wealth Tax Act are concerned: a sub-section (3) has been added to sections 278B and 35HA, respectively, that came into force from 1st October, 2004, by the Finance Act (No.2) 2004, reading-"Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a person, being a company, and the punishment for such offence is imprisonment and fine, then, without prejudice to the provisions in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), such company shall be punished with fine and every person referred to in sub-section (1) or the director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company referred to in sub-section (2), shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished in accordance with the provisions of the Act". From the point of accountability of companies to the society at large with their great resource-backed potential for mischief it is unfortunate, the trend set in law of attribution of culpability to the company as such in our country is just to let it go with fine and nothing more to it. This development seems to be the result of the majority decision of the three member bench in Asstt. Commissioner v. Velliappa Textiles 2003 AIR SCW 5647, saying that a company cannot be prosecuted if the provision in law is punishment by imprisonment only. It is unfortunate because even in the present day modern social order it is difficult to assume that the King can do no wrong or that all of His wrongs are off in a money-wash, and a company and its directors being far less privileged than a King at any rate, some other alternative provision in law, may be business inhibitory in nature and commensurate to the seriousness of the economic offence involved at least for a short run of time, ought to be attributable to the company that stigmatises the directors automatically, in the interest of natural justice to curb the obsession with public mischief for private profit in disguise.

11.10-9a The trend has been stalled by Supreme Court - However, the later decision of Supreme Court in Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 275 ITR 81/145 Taxman 154 to the effect that there is no immunity to the companies from prosecution merely because the prosecution is in respect of offences for which the punishment prescribed is mandatory imprisonment, seems to be rational and correct, both in itself and constitutionally.

Background of ‘Standard Chartered’ majority verdict

11.10-10 The 2:1 decision of the three Judge Bench in Velliappa’s case is said to be in line with the Law Commission recommendation made in its 41st and 47th Reports suggesting amendments to the Acts relating to economic offences and the IPC to say that offences punishable with only imprisonment or imprisonment and fine means only fine when the offender is a company or corporation, leading to an amendment proposed to the IPC in 1972 that had lapsed. The majority decision in Velliappa’s case was based on the Act provision being mandatory imprisonment plus fine, leaving no choice to the Court to impose only fine in lieu of imprisonment, leading to the conclusion that a company cannot be prosecuted for such offences until the Act is amended as was done in Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Netherlands and the EU, on the footing that it is not Court’s function "to repair the blunders that are to be found in legislation. They must be corrected by the Legislature": Bristol Guardians v. Bristol Waterworks Co. (1914) AC 379. The minority judgment given by Mathur J. in the said case was that the Court would be shrinking from its responsibility of imparting justice by the conclusion that a juristic person like a company cannot be sent to jail and therefore it is free from prosecution even for serious offences which only attract mandatory imprisonment in law. The verdict of the 3-Judge Bench in ANZ Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Directorate of Enforcement [2005] 58 SCL 350 (SC) doubted the correctness of the majority verdict in Velliappa’s case; and in Standard Chartered case, cited above, a 5-Judge Bench gave the verdict with 3:2 majority that companies or corporations cannot go scot-free having committed serious offences, and it also cannot be the intention of the Legislature to grant blanket immunity in that fashion, and in that view of the matter it was taken that discretion is given to the Court to impose prison sentence or fine in such cases, over-ruling the Velliappa precedent.

Person- in-charge and responsible to the company

In the case of a company and particularly a public limited company the person-in-charge of the company and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company are the board of directors. In other words every director of a company is a person in-charge of the company and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business (Ashok Leyland Finance Ltd. v. R. S. Aggarwal (2003) 10 Scale 1000). But every director is not responsible for an offence. In Smt. Katta Sujatha v. Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Ltd. [2002] 7 SCC 655, the Supreme Court observed that a person could be a party to the policy being followed by a company and yet not be in-charge of the business of a company or that a person may be in-charge of a company but not in overall charge or that a person may be in-charge of only some part of the business of the company. The Supreme Court laid down that not all the directors of a company will be responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. This has been so held despite the general law that a company is governed by the board of directors. Apart from being a director, the accused director also need to have been involved either in the management of the specific part of the business of the company relating to the offence or he should be in actual overall control of the business and not merely a member of the board of directors or responsible for the conduct of the business of the company by virtue of being a director of the company only [see Everest Advertising (P.) Ltd. v. State [2005] 128 Comp. Cas. 787 (Delhi)]

Person-in-charge means that the person should be in control of the day- to-day business of the company [See Girdharilal Gupta v. D. N. Mehta AIR 1971 SC 2162 and State of Karnataka v. Pratap Chand [1981] 128 ITR 573 (SC)]. The Supreme Court in Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana [1990] 67 Comp. Cas. 1 observed that all the partners of a firm are not liable for an offence committed by the firm irrespective of whether they were running the business or not, and that it would be a travesty of justice to prosecute all the partners and ask them to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge.

A person is said to be responsible to the company for the conduct of the business if he has the control and authority over the conduct of the business and the duty to take care in respect thereof. Lord Diplock observed in Tesco Supermarkets Ltd. v. Nattras (1972) AC 153 (HL), as follows:

"in my view, therefore, the question : what natural persons are to be treated in law as being the company for the purpose of acts done in the course of its business, including the taking of precautions and exercise of due diligence to avoid the commission of a criminal offence, is to be found by identifying the natural persons who by the memorandum and articles of association or as a result of action taken by the directors, or by the company in general meeting pursuant to the articles, are entrusted with the exercise of the powers of the company."

Thus, all directors of the company will be officer in default only when there is no managing director, whole-time director, a manager or secretary, a person charged by the board with the responsibility of complying with the provisions of the Act and the director/directors specified by the board [see Vijay Kumar Gupta v. Registrar of Company (2003) CLC 777 (HP)]. For an officer who is in default and liable to be punished he must first be an officer of the company and then he must be in default. For violation of a particular provision, it is necessary to identify the officer who has committed the default [see H. Nanjundiah v. V. Govindan [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 356 (Bom.) ; and S. P. Punj v. ROC [1991] 71 Comp. Cas. 509 (Delhi)]. Where in a complaint, accused were not shown as "officer in default" they could not be held responsible merely because they were directors [see Ramesh Chandra Manilal Kotla v. State of Gujarat (1998) 30 CLA 313 (Guj.). In Sham Sunder v. State of Haryana [1990] 67 Comp. Cas. 1], the Supreme Court observed that all the partners of a firm are not liable for an offence committed by the firm irrespective of whether they were running the business or not, and it would be travesty of justice prosecute all the partners and ask them to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge. The obligation on the accused to prove that the offence took place without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent such offence arises only when the prosecution establishes that the requisite conditions mentioned in the relevant section is established. The ratio of the case is applicable in the case of a company also. A director who was neither a managing or whole-time director nor was involved in day-to-day affairs of the company cannot be said to be an officer in default [see H. Nanjundiah v. Govindan, Registrar of Companies [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 356 (Bom.)].
